abstract: Photonic time-delayed reservoir computing (TDRC) based on conventional Class B lasers is limited by fragile external cavity mode (ECM) locking dynamics. Here, we show that engineering the polarization lifetime (T$_2$) with the carrier lifetime ($T$) reshapes the topology and stability of TDRC. Comparing four laser classes (Class A, Class B, Class C$_A$, and Class C$_B$), a finite polarization lifetime acts as an intrinsic dynamic filter, dissolving discrete ECM chaos grids into continuous, phase-tolerant operational basins. Information processing capacity (IPC) decomposition further exposes distinct computational profiles: matched Class C$_A$ achieves the highest nonlinear capacity (16.28) and the highest total capacity (19.29), whereas Class A exhibits the highest linear capacity (4.70). A task-dependent reversal governs hardware design: Class A and Class C$_A$ achieve comparable, and the lowest, NRMSE on short-horizon Mackey--Glass prediction (0.0103 and 0.0105, within one standard deviation), while the time-scale-matched Class C$_A$ dominates the higher-dimensional Lorenz (0.0506) and the experimental Santa Fe (0.4251) tasks. Linear-IPC ranking matches Mackey-Glass accuracy; nonlinear-IPC ranking matches the Lorenz exactly and Santa Fe within the mask-to-mask uncertainty. Under realistic quantum noise, resilience is dictated mainly by $T$, not T$_2$: Class A retains the lowest NRMSE (0.47) even at spontaneous emission factor $β$ = $10^{-1}$, whereas the long-carrier Class B degrades (0.98). A residual T$_2$-mediated benefit of 20$\%$ persists in the slow-carrier Class C$_B$ (0.78 vs. 0.98). Time-scale engineering thus offers a nuanced design paradigm for optical computing, where optimal hardware is set by the task's time-scale hierarchy rather than a universal figure of merit.
